summary: Defines version 2 of the protocol operations for SNMP, including the syntax and the procedures for sending, receiving and processing SNMP PDUs. It is the part of the framework that describes the actual requests and responses between managers and agents. It replaces RFC 1905.

eli5.summary: This is the list of questions and commands a network manager can send to a device, plus the way devices must answer. It is the basic conversation rulebook.

subtitle: The requests, responses and notifications a network manager and a managed device use to talk SNMP, and exactly how each one is processed.

tldr.problem: A management station needs a precise, interoperable way to read, change and be told about values on devices, without each vendor inventing its own conversation.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the SNMPv2 PDU formats in ASN.1 and the processing rules for Get, GetNext, GetBulk, Set, Response, Trap and Inform operations, each carrying a list of variable bindings.
tldr.outcome: It is an Internet Standard (STD 62) that replaces RFC 1905 with no change to the protocol itself, and it has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 3416 is an Internet Standard (STD 62) and is not obsoleted or updated by any later RFC listed for it. It replaced RFC 1905, and it is companion to RFC 3418, which defines the MIB objects these operations refer to.

sections.title: Where the Operations Fit
sections.content:
The SNMP Management Framework has five components: an architecture, a way of describing managed objects (the SMI), message protocols, protocol operations and a set of fundamental applications. RFC 3416 is the protocol operations piece. It defines what is sent and received, while the message protocol carries those PDUs.

Managed objects live in a virtual information store called the Management Information Base (MIB). Entities that run command generator or notification receiver applications are traditionally called managers. Entities that run command responder or notification originator applications are traditionally called agents. The stated purpose of the protocol is the transport of management information and operations.
sections.eli5: There is a big notebook of facts about each device. This RFC explains the questions a manager may ask about that notebook and how the device must reply.

sections.title: Variables, Retransmission and Message Size
sections.content:
A variable binding pairs the name of a variable with its value. A variable name is an OBJECT IDENTIFIER: the identifier of the object type followed by a fragment that names the instance. A list of bindings is a variable-binding list. SNMP limits an OBJECT IDENTIFIER to at most 128 sub-identifiers, each with a maximum value of 2**32-1.

Every request normally gets a response. Whether to retransmit an unanswered request is up to the originating application, but it must act responsibly about how often and for how long, and the RFC points to BCP 41 (RFC 2914) on congestion control.

The size of a message is limited to the smaller of what the destination can accept and what the source can generate. A conformant implementation must never send a message larger than the receiver allows. Large GetBulk replies may exceed the path MTU and be fragmented, which the RFC calls harmful, so a sender should use only small max-repetitions values when the network is under stress.

SNMP needs only an unreliable datagram service, with each message entirely contained in one transport datagram. The preferred mapping is UDP (RFC 768).
sections.eli5: Every question gets an answer. If no answer comes you may ask again, but you should not nag. Also, your question and the answer must fit in an envelope that both sides can handle.

sections.title: The PDU Syntax
sections.content:
The PDUs are defined in ASN.1 in a module called SNMPv2-PDU. Values are either simple (a 32-bit signed integer, an OCTET STRING of 0 to 65535 bytes, or an OBJECT IDENTIFIER) or application-wide (IpAddress, Counter32, TimeTicks, Opaque, Counter64, Unsigned32). The SMIv2 BITS construct is encoded as an OCTET STRING, with named bits placed from the high-order bit of the first octet onward and unused trailing bits set to zero.

Most PDUs share one shape with four fields: request-id, error-status, error-index and variable-bindings. The GetBulk request has the same structure, but its second and third fields are non-repeaters and max-repetitions. The number of bindings may be up to max-bindings, which is 2147483647.

The error-status field has 19 values, from noError(0) and tooBig(1) to inconsistentName(18). Three of them, noSuchName, badValue and readOnly, exist for proxy compatibility. In a binding, a value may be unSpecified (used in retrieval requests), or one of the exceptions noSuchObject, noSuchInstance and endOfMibView in responses.
sections.eli5: Every message uses the same form: a ticket number, an error box, and a list of name and value pairs. Different messages just fill the form in different ways.

sections.title: Reading: Get, GetNext and GetBulk
sections.content:
Any field a procedure does not use is ignored, but all of a PDU must still be valid ASN.1. A compliant implementation must support as many bindings as fit in the maximum message size, up to 2147483647.

GetRequest looks up each name exactly. If the name matches an accessible variable, its value is returned. If no variable has a matching OBJECT IDENTIFIER prefix, the value is noSuchObject. Otherwise it is noSuchInstance. A failure for any other reason gives genErr with error-index set to the failed binding.

GetNextRequest returns, for each name, the first lexicographic successor among accessible variables. If there is none, the value is endOfMibView. This is how a manager walks a table: it keeps asking for the next name after the one it last received. When it runs off the end of a table, the answer is the next object outside it.

GetBulkRequest is designed to retrieve a large amount of data in few exchanges. The first N bindings (N is the smaller of non-repeaters and the number of bindings sent) each get one successor. Each of the remaining R bindings is repeated M times, where M is max-repetitions, so the total requested is N + (M * R). The reply may be shorter if it would not fit in the message, if every binding in some iteration is endOfMibView, or if the responder cuts off a request that needs far too much processing time (at least one repetition must be completed).

In all three, if the reply would exceed a local constraint or the originator's maximum message size, the responder sends an alternate Response with tooBig, error-index zero and no bindings. If even that is too large, the snmpSilentDrops counter is incremented and the message is discarded.
sections.eli5: Get is asking about one specific thing. GetNext is saying "what comes after this?", which lets you walk through a long list one item at a time. GetBulk is saying "give me the next several things at once" so you ask fewer times.

sections.title: Writing: SetRequest and Response
sections.content:
A Response-PDU is generated only in answer to a Get, GetNext, GetBulk, Set or Inform request. It copies the request's request-id, which lets the sender match answers to outstanding requests and spot network duplicates. If a retransmission reuses the same request-id, either answer satisfies it, but a different request-id is recommended in most cases so that round-trip time can be measured. A non-zero error-status means the request failed, and then error-index gives the one-based position of the offending binding.

SetRequest is processed in two conceptual phases. First, each binding is validated in order, and the first failure picks the error: noAccess, notWritable, wrongType, wrongLength, wrongEncoding, wrongValue, noCreation, inconsistentName, inconsistentValue, resourceUnavailable or genErr. Second, if all passed, the assignments happen as if simultaneously.

If an assignment still fails, all the others are undone and the status is commitFailed. Only if the undo is impossible is the status undoFailed with error-index zero. Implementations are strongly encouraged to avoid both codes. Naming one variable twice with different values gives an implementation-specific result.
sections.eli5: When you ask someone to change several things, they first check that every change is allowed. Only if all are fine do they make them. If one goes wrong halfway, they put everything back the way it was.

sections.title: Notifications: Trap and Inform
sections.content:
Devices can speak first. An SNMPv2-Trap-PDU tells a notification receiver that an event happened or a condition exists. There is no confirmation. Where it is sent is implementation-dependent.

An InformRequest-PDU carries the same kind of news but is confirmed: the receiver passes the contents to its application and returns a Response with noError. The RFC adds that there is still no guarantee of delivery. If the response would be too big, the receiver sends the tooBig alternate response, as for the other requests.

In both, the first two bindings are sysUpTime.0 and snmpTrapOID.0, both from RFC 3418 (RFC 3418). Next come the variables named in the OBJECTS clause of the notification definition, in order, and then any extra variables the sender chooses to include. A Report-PDU exists in the syntax, but its semantics are left to whichever administrative framework uses it.
sections.eli5: A trap is a device shouting "something happened!" without waiting to hear back. An inform is the same shout, but the listener has to say "got it."

sections.title: Security
sections.content:
The protocol on its own does not give a secure environment. Even if the network is secure, for example with IPSec, nothing controls who on that network may access management information.

The RFC recommends the SNMPv3 security features, specifically the User-based Security Model (RFC 3414) and the View-based Access Control Model (RFC 3415). It is then up to the customer or user to configure the entity so that only legitimate principals can read or change MIB objects, that events are communicated appropriately, and that the entity treats incoming information with due credence.
sections.eli5: The rules for asking questions do not include a lock. You have to add locks from the other SNMP rules and set them up yourself.

sections.title: Changes from RFC 1905
sections.content:
This document obsoletes RFC 1905. The RFC lists many editorial updates: a table of contents, an abstract, an intellectual property notice, a rewritten introduction, and terminology moved from manager/agent to the architecture's terms. It also says most protocol-related edits do not affect the protocol.

Notable clarifications include how many variable bindings an implementation must support, the handling of BITS, consistent handling of extra bindings in informs and traps, notes on the two ways of reaching the end of a table in the examples, a new reference to RFC 2914, and expanded security considerations.
sections.eli5: This is a tidied-up second edition. The wording is cleaner, but the way devices talk did not change.
